topic: How 99% of the Internet Crosses the Ocean Floor
angle: We call the internet 'the cloud,' but 99% of global data actually travels through hair-thin glass strands resting miles deep on the pitch-black ocean floor.
why: Proven by massive demand for physical infrastructure explainers like Veritasium's 14.5M views on fiber optics and Mr Decode's 19.7M views on sub-aquatic engineering. It shatters the universal misconception that modern internet runs through space satellites, revealing the astonishing physical machinery sitting under our oceans.

fiber optic cables under the ocean

facts: Over 95% to 99% of all intercontinental internet traffic travels through subsea fiber optic cables, not satellites.
There are more than 550 active and planned undersea cables spanning roughly 1.4 million kilometers (around 870,000 miles) across the globe.
In deep ocean waters, the cable is surprisingly thin—typically only 17 to 20 millimeters in diameter, roughly the thickness of an ordinary garden hose.
Near shorelines and shallow waters, cables are armored with multiple layers of galvanized steel wire and tar, swelling to the thickness of a soda can to resist boat anchors and fishing nets.
The data-carrying core consists of hair-thin strands of ultra-pure silica glass that transmit digital information as pulses of laser light.
Light pulses inside optical fibers travel at roughly 200,000 kilometers per second (about two-thirds the speed of light in a vacuum).
Because light naturally dims over long distances in glass, optical repeaters are spliced into the cable every 50 to 100 kilometers to re-amplify the optical signal.
These repeaters are powered by a continuous copper conductor inside the cable that carries up to 10,000 to 15,000 volts of direct current (DC) delivered from coastal terminal stations.
Specialized cable-laying ships carry thousands of miles of coiled cable in giant internal carousels, spooling it out continuously 24 hours a day while crossing the ocean.
In shallow coastal waters, a heavy sea plow towed behind the ship slices a trench into the seabed and buries the cable up to 3 meters deep to protect it.
In the deep ocean (down to depths of 8,000 meters / 26,000 feet), the cable simply rests directly on the abyssal plain due to its own weight and the complete absence of human disturbance.
Roughly 70% of all submarine cable damage is caused by commercial fishing trawlers and dragged ship anchors, while underwater earthquakes and mudslides cause most of the rest.
Shark bites on subsea cables are extremely rare; modern cables use steel armoring and dense polyethylene insulation that prevents electrical leakage from attracting marine life.
When a cable breaks, engineers pinpoint the fault location within meters from land by firing laser pulses into the fiber and measuring the reflection time (Optical Time-Domain Reflectometry).
Repair ships lower specialized grapnel hooks or robotic ROVs to cut and retrieve the severed cable ends, bringing them up to the ship's deck.
Technicians on board splice replacement glass fibers inside sterile, climate-controlled clean rooms before lowering the repaired line back to the seafloor.
A single modern subsea cable, such as Google's Dunant or Grace Hopper, can transmit over 250 to 350 terabits of data per second across an entire ocean.
